records.source: Πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως πάλαι ὁ θεὸς λαλήσας τοῖς πατράσιν ἐν τοῖς προφήταις ἐπ’ ἐσχάτου τῶν ἡμερῶν τούτων ἐλάλησεν ἡμῖν ἐν υἱῷ, ὃν ἔθηκεν κληρονόμον πάντων, δι’ οὗ καὶ ἐποίησεν τοὺς αἰῶνας·
records.gloss: In many portions and in many ways long ago the God having spoken to the fathers in the prophets \v 2 at [the] last of the days these spoke to us in [a] Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the ages;
pieces: Long ago God spoke to the {{gender:ancestors|fathers}} through the prophets, in many separate portions and by many different means.

But at the end of these days {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has spoken to us through the Son, whom {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} appointed heir of all things and through whom {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} also made the ages.

L.1: In many portions and in many ways long ago God, having spoken to the fathers by the prophets,
L.2: at the last of these days has spoken to us by [a] Son, whom {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} appointed heir of all things, through whom {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} also made the ages;

R.1: Long ago God spoke to our {{gender:ancestors|fathers}} through the prophets. He spoke to them bit by bit and in many different ways.
R.2: But now, in these last days, God has spoken to us through {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Son. God chose the Son to receive everything as {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} heir. Through the Son God also made the world and all its ages.

decisions.choice: one long sentence: verses 1-4 are a single sentence that continues into verse 3 with "who"
decisions.reason: In the Greek, verses 1-4 are one carefully built sentence. Its main statement is that God, who once spoke through the prophets, has now spoken in a Son; everything after that describes the Son, joined by "whom", "through whom" and then "who" (verse 3). The SBL text puts a raised dot after "the ages", so this record ends there and verse 3 begins a new one, but the thought runs on without a break. The renderings may break it into shorter sentences; they do not change how the clauses depend on one another.

decisions.choice: in many portions and in many ways: God's earlier speaking came piece by piece and by varied means
alternatives: at many times and in various ways (taking the first word of time)
decisions.reason: πολυμερῶς means "in many parts or installments", πολυτρόπως "in many manners". God spoke over many centuries, a part at a time, and by many means: laws, visions, dreams, events and the prophets' words (compare Numbers 12:6-8). The two words prepare the contrast with the one, final word spoken in a Son.

decisions.choice: at the last of these days: in the final age that has now begun
alternatives: at the end of the world
decisions.reason: "The last days" is an Old Testament phrase for the time when God would fulfill his promises (Numbers 24:14; Isaiah 2:2; Hosea 3:5). The author says those days are "these" days: the age of fulfillment has arrived with the Son.

decisions.choice: by a Son: through one who is Son, in contrast with the prophets
alternatives: in his Son (as if the article stood there)
decisions.reason: There is no article before υἱῷ. The author stresses what kind of messenger God used this time: not a prophet but one who is Son. ἐν here has the sense "by, through, in the person of", as with "by the prophets" in verse 1. Chapter 1 goes on to show from Scripture what being "Son" means (verse 5).

decisions.choice: appointed heir of all things: echoes Psalm 2:8
decisions.reason: In Psalm 2 God tells the king he calls "my Son" (Psalm 2:7, quoted in verse 5) that he will give him the nations as his inheritance and the ends of the earth as his possession (Psalm 2:8). The Son is heir not of a land only but of "all things". The theme of inheriting runs on in verse 4 ("inherited a name") and verse 14.

decisions.choice: the ages: the created universe seen as the whole course of its time and all it contains
decisions.reason: αἰών means "age, a long period of time"; in the plural it can stand for the world itself, the universe taken as the sum of its ages and everything in them, much as the Hebrew word for "age" came to mean "world". Hebrews uses the same phrase again in 11:3, where "the ages" were fashioned by the word of God. The Son is the one through whom God made everything that exists across all time (compare John 1:3; Colossians 1:16).

decisions.choice: {{gender:ancestors|fathers}}
decisions.reason: The fathers are the ancestors of Israel, women as well as men, to whom God spoke through the prophets, so the gender setting applies; "fathers" is the traditional alternative. Literal keeps "the fathers".

decisions.choice: by [a] Son (L); through the Son (B); through {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Son (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the missing article with "[a] Son". "Through a Son" reads oddly in natural speech, so Balanced uses "the Son", the title by which the chapter names him, and Readable "his Son". The point of the missing article, that this messenger is Son and not a prophet, is given in meaning decision m4. "Son" is capitalized as a title of Christ.

decisions.choice: our {{gender:ancestors|fathers}}; the world and all its ages
decisions.reason: Readable adds "our", since the readers are heirs of Israel's story, and explains "the ages" as "the world and all its ages" so that a young reader does not hear only "periods of time" (see m6).

records.heading: God has spoken by the Son

records.source: ὃς ὢν ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ, φέρων τε τὰ πάντα τῷ ῥήματι τῆς δυνάμεως, δι’ αὑτοῦ καθαρισμὸν τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ποιησάμενος ἐκάθισεν ἐν δεξιᾷ τῆς μεγαλωσύνης ἐν ὑψηλοῖς, τοσούτῳ κρείττων γενόμενος τῶν ἀγγέλων ὅσῳ διαφορώτερον παρ’ αὐτοὺς κεκληρονόμηκεν ὄνομα.
records.gloss: who being radiance of the glory and stamp of the essence of him, bearing and the all things by the word of the power, through himself purification of the sins having made sat down at [the] right [hand] of the majesty in high [places], \v 4 by so much better having become than the angels as much as more excellent beyond them he has inherited [a] name.
pieces: The Son is the radiance of God's glory and the exact stamp of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} being, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} bears all things along by {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} word of power. Having made cleansing for sins through {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} took {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} seat at the right hand of the Majesty on high.
So {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has become far better than the angels, as far as the name that is {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} by inheritance excels theirs.

L.3: who, being [the] radiance of the glory and [the] stamp of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} essence, and bearing all things by the word of power, having made purification of sins through {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}, sat down at [the] right [hand] of the Majesty on high,
L.4: having become so much better than the angels as the name {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has inherited [is] more excellent than theirs.

R.3: The Son is the bright shining of God's glory. He is the exact likeness of God's very being. He carries all things along by {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} powerful word. He made people clean from their sins. Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} sat down at the right hand of God, the Majesty in heaven, the place of highest honor.
R.4: So the Son became far greater than the angels, just as the name {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} received from God is far greater than theirs.

decisions.choice: the word of power, having made purification through himself (SBLGNT)
alternatives: by the word of his power, having made purification of sins
having made purification of our sins through himself
decisions.reason: The SBL text reads "by the word of power, through himself having made purification of sins", with no "his" after "power". This follows the oldest papyrus of Hebrews (P46), which can be read as taking the pronoun after "power" as "through himself". Many manuscripts read "by the word of his power, having made purification of sins", and the later majority of manuscripts have "by the word of his power, having made purification of our sins through himself". The sense hardly changes: the word of power is the Son's, and he made the cleansing himself. This description is from general knowledge; reviewers must check it against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: radiance: the brightness that shines out from God's glory
decisions.reason: ἀπαύγασμα can mean light shining out from a source ("radiance") or light thrown back ("reflection"). The active sense fits better: the Son is not a copy lit from outside but the shining of God's own glory, as light is one with its source. The same word is used of Wisdom in Wisdom of Solomon 7:26, a book in the Greek Old Testament, and the author may be echoing it.

decisions.choice: stamp: the exact impression, like the image a die stamps on a coin
decisions.reason: χαρακτήρ was the mark made by a seal or a die, and so an exact representation of the original. The Son shows precisely what God is, as a coin bears the exact design of the die. The word occurs only here in the New Testament.

decisions.choice: essence, being: the underlying reality of what God is
decisions.reason: ὑπόστασις means literally "what stands under", the real substance of a thing. Here it is God's own being, his essential nature, of which the Son is the exact stamp. Hebrews uses the same word in other senses at 3:14 ("confidence") and 11:1 ("assurance"). In the fourth century, church councils used this word for each "person" of the Trinity; that later technical sense is not what it means here, where it is God's being as a whole.

decisions.choice: bearing: carrying all things along, sustaining and guiding them
decisions.reason: φέρω means "carry, bear". The Son does not only hold the universe up as a weight; he carries it forward on its course, by the same powerful word through which God made it (1:2; 11:3).

decisions.choice: purification of sins, then seated at God's right hand: Psalm 110:1 and the Day of Atonement
decisions.reason: "Sat down at the right hand" takes up Psalm 110:1, which verse 13 quotes. "Purification of sins" is the language of the Day of Atonement, when the high priest's sacrifice was to cleanse Israel from all their sins (Leviticus 16:30); chapters 9-10 develop it. Unlike the priests who stood day after day (10:11-12), the Son sat down, because the work was finished. "The Majesty on high" is a reverent way of naming God.

decisions.choice: having become better: the Son, after his work, was enthroned above the angels; the name is "Son"
decisions.reason: "Having become" refers to the Son's enthronement after he made purification for sins, not to a time when he was less than the angels in himself; verses 2-3 have already said he made the ages and is the radiance of God's glory. Chapter 2 explains that for a little while he was made lower than the angels and was then crowned (2:9). The name he has inherited is most likely "Son", the name verse 5 says God never gave to any angel. κρείττων ("better, superior") is a word Hebrews comes back to often: a better hope, a better covenant, better promises (7:19, 7:22, 8:6).

decisions.choice: being
decisions.reason: Literal says "essence" to show that the word names the underlying reality of God; Balanced and Readable say "being" (Readable "very being"), which says the same in more common words.

decisions.choice: The Son ... God's glory
alternatives: He is the radiance of the glory
decisions.reason: The Greek begins with "who" and says "the glory". Since this record starts a new sentence, Balanced and Readable name "the Son" and make clear that the glory is God's.

decisions.choice: better
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced say "better", because the same word marks the author's argument through the letter (better hope, better covenant, better sacrifices) and a reader can follow it. Readable says "greater", which is plainer here.

decisions.choice: the place of highest honor; received from God
decisions.reason: Readable explains that the right hand of a king was the place of highest honor and power, and says that the name was received from God, since "inherit" here means to receive as one's own.

records.source: Τίνι γὰρ εἶπέν ποτε τῶν ἀγγέλων· Υἱός μου εἶ σύ, ἐγὼ σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε, καὶ πάλιν· Ἐγὼ ἔσομαι αὐτῷ εἰς πατέρα, καὶ αὐτὸς ἔσται μοι εἰς υἱόν;
records.gloss: To which for did he say ever of the angels, Son of me are you, I today have begotten you, and again, I will be to him for father, and he will be to me for son?
pieces: For to which of the angels did God ever say, "You are {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} Son; this very day I have fathered {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}"? Or again, "I will be a Father to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will be a Son to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}"?

L.5: For to which of the angels did {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} ever say, "You are {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} Son; I today have begotten {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}"? And again, "I will be to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} for a Father, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will be to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} for a Son"?

R.5: God never said to any angel, "You are {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} Son. Today I have fathered {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}." And God never said about an angel, "I will be a Father to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will be a Son to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}."

decisions.choice: Psalm 2:7
decisions.reason: The first quotation is Psalm 2:7. Psalm 2 is a royal psalm: God installs his king on Zion and declares him his son, probably on the day of his enthronement. The New Testament applies it to Jesus' resurrection and exaltation (Acts 13:33), and Hebrews quotes it again at 5:5.

decisions.choice: I have begotten you: God declares and installs the Son as king
alternatives: today I have become your Father (a free paraphrase)
decisions.reason: γεννάω is a father's act, "beget, become father of". In Psalm 2 it is figurative: on the day of his enthronement the king became God's son in a royal sense. The author applies it to the Son's exaltation (1:3-4), not to a beginning of his existence, since verse 2 has already said the ages were made through him.

decisions.choice: fathered
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the traditional "begotten"; Balanced and Readable say "fathered", the everyday word for the same act, as Hebrews 5:5 does where the same verse of Psalm 2 is quoted again (m2 explains that it is figurative).

decisions.choice: 2 Samuel 7:14 (also 1 Chronicles 17:13)
decisions.reason: The second quotation is God's promise to David through Nathan about David's son who would build God's house: "I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me" (2 Samuel 7:14; 1 Chronicles 17:13). The author reads it of the Son, the heir of David's throne.

decisions.choice: a question expecting the answer "none"
decisions.reason: The question is rhetorical: God never addressed any single angel as "my Son". Angels as a group can be called "sons of God" in the Hebrew text (Job 1:6), but the Greek translation often has "angels of God" there, and no angel is ever given this title personally. The same question closes the quotations at verse 13.

decisions.choice: God
decisions.reason: The Greek says only "did he say"; the speaker is God, as in verse 1, so Balanced and Readable name him.

decisions.choice: Son, Father (capitalized)
decisions.reason: In these quotations the author applies "son" to Christ and "father" to God, so both are capitalized as titles. Pronouns for God and for the Son take the deity_pronoun setting.

decisions.choice: God never said to any angel
alternatives: To which of the angels did God ever say
decisions.reason: Readable turns the rhetorical question into the statement it implies, so that a young reader does not miss the point.

records.heading: The Son is greater than the angels

records.source: ὅταν δὲ πάλιν εἰσαγάγῃ τὸν πρωτότοκον εἰς τὴν οἰκουμένην, λέγει· Καὶ προσκυνησάτωσαν αὐτῷ πάντες ἄγγελοι θεοῦ.
records.gloss: When and again he brings in the firstborn into the inhabited world, he says, And let worship him all angels of God.
pieces: And again, at the time God brings {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} firstborn into the world, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says, "All the angels of God are to worship {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}."

L.6: And when again {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} brings the firstborn into the inhabited world, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says, "And let all [the] angels of God worship {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}."

R.6: In another place, when God brings {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} firstborn Son into the world, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says, "All of God's angels must worship {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}."

decisions.choice: again: introduces another quotation, as in verse 5
alternatives: when he brings the firstborn into the world again
decisions.reason: πάλιν could go with the verb ("when he again brings the firstborn into the world", that is, at his second coming) or introduce the next quotation ("and again"), as it does in 1:5, 2:13 and 10:30. Its place inside the "when" clause favors the first reading, but the author's habit favors the second, and nothing elsewhere in the chapter speaks of a second coming. Literal keeps the Greek order.

decisions.choice: brings the firstborn into the world: the Son's entry into his rule, most likely his enthronement
decisions.reason: The text does not say which event is meant. It may be the Son's birth into the world, his exaltation and enthronement (1:3-4, 1:13), or his return. The word for "world" comes back in 2:5 for "the world to come", which God has subjected to the Son and not to angels; that suggests the enthronement, when the angels are told to worship him.

decisions.choice: firstborn: the son with the rank and rights of the heir
decisions.reason: πρωτότοκος is a title of rank more than of birth order. God says of David's heir, "I will make him the firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth" (Psalm 89:28). It fits the Son as "heir of all things" (1:2).

decisions.choice: the inhabited world: the world of people and nations
decisions.reason: οἰκουμένη means the inhabited earth, the world of human beings. In 2:5 the author speaks of "the coming inhabited world", the new order over which the Son rules.

decisions.choice: Deuteronomy 32:43 (Greek); compare Psalm 97:7 (96:7 Greek)
decisions.reason: The words come from the Song of Moses in its Greek form, Deuteronomy 32:43: "let all the angels of God worship him". The standard Hebrew text of Deuteronomy 32:43 has no such line; a Hebrew manuscript of Deuteronomy from the Dead Sea Scrolls has "bow down to him, all gods". Psalm 97:7 (96:7 Greek) has a similar call to worship. In the Song, God is the one worshiped; the author applies the words to the Son.

decisions.choice: the world
decisions.reason: Literal says "the inhabited world" for this word, here and at 2:5; Balanced and Readable say "the world", which is how the word is normally heard.

decisions.choice: God ... {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} firstborn (R: {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} firstborn Son)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name God as the subject, and say "his firstborn"; Readable adds "Son" so that the reader knows who the firstborn is.

records.source: καὶ πρὸς μὲν τοὺς ἀγγέλους λέγει· Ὁ ποιῶν τοὺς ἀγγέλους αὐτοῦ πνεύματα, καὶ τοὺς λειτουργοὺς αὐτοῦ πυρὸς φλόγα·
records.gloss: And to indeed the angels he says, The [one] making the angels of him winds, and the ministers of him of fire a flame;
pieces: About the angels {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says, "He turns {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} angels into winds, and those who serve {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} into a flame of fire."

L.7: And with regard to the angels {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says, "The one making {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} angels winds, and {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} ministers a flame of fire";

R.7: This is what God says about the angels: "He makes {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} angels into winds. He makes {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} servants into flames of fire."

decisions.choice: Psalm 104:4 (103:4 Greek)
decisions.reason: The quotation follows the Greek of Psalm 104:4 (103:4 in its numbering). The Hebrew is most naturally read "he makes winds his messengers, flames of fire his servants": the winds and the lightning serve God. The Greek reads it the other way round, "he makes his angels winds", and the author uses that form: angels are changeable servants whom God can turn into wind and fire, while the Son's throne lasts forever (verse 8).

decisions.choice: winds
decisions.reason: πνεῦμα means both "wind" and "spirit". In the psalm, which speaks of clouds, wind and fire, "winds" fits the parallel with "flame of fire". In verse 14 the same word in the plural describes the angels as "spirits" who serve.

decisions.choice: ministers: those who carry out sacred service
decisions.reason: λειτουργός is a servant who performs public, often sacred, service. Hebrews uses the word for Christ as minister of the true sanctuary (8:2), and the related adjective for the angels in verse 14.

decisions.choice: with regard to the angels
decisions.reason: πρός here means "with reference to": the psalm is not spoken to the angels but about them. With μέν it sets up the contrast "but to the Son" in verse 8.

decisions.choice: He turns ... into
decisions.reason: Balanced renders the construction "making X into Y" as "turns ... into", which says plainly that God gives the angels the form of wind and fire.

records.source: πρὸς δὲ τὸν υἱόν· Ὁ θρόνος σου ὁ θεὸς εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τοῦ αἰῶνος, καὶ ἡ ῥάβδος τῆς εὐθύτητος ῥάβδος τῆς βασιλείας σου.
records.gloss: To but the Son, The throne of you, the God, to the age of the age, and the scepter of the uprightness [is] scepter of the kingdom of you.
pieces: But to the Son {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says, "Your throne, O God, lasts forever and ever, and the scepter of {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} kingdom is a scepter of uprightness.

L.8: But to the Son: "Your throne, O God, [is] forever and ever, and the scepter of uprightness [is the] scepter of {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} kingdom.

R.8: But God says this to the Son: "O God, {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} throne will last forever and ever. You rule {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} kingdom with what is right and fair.

decisions.choice: Psalm 45:7-8 (44:7-8 Greek)
decisions.reason: Verses 8-9 quote Psalm 45:7-8 (44:7-8 in the Greek numbering), a song for the wedding of the king. The psalm addresses the king in exalted terms; the author hears in it God speaking to the Son, whose throne is everlasting.

decisions.choice: O God: the Son is addressed as God
alternatives: God is your throne forever and ever
your throne is God's throne forever
decisions.reason: ὁ θεὸς can be read as an address ("Your throne, O God, is forever") or as the predicate ("Your throne is God forever", or "God is your throne"). The Hebrew of Psalm 45:7 is most naturally an address to the king as "God", and the author's contrast fits it: the angels are servants, but the Son is addressed as God and has an everlasting throne.

decisions.choice: your kingdom (SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: The SBL text reads "the scepter of your kingdom", as the Greek psalm does and as most manuscripts have it. Some of the oldest manuscripts (P46, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) read "his kingdom", which would favor taking "God" as the subject earlier in the verse ("God is your throne ... and the scepter of uprightness is the scepter of his kingdom"). This description is from general knowledge; reviewers must check it against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: to the age of the age: forever and ever
decisions.reason: "To the age of the age" is a Hebrew way of saying "forever", made stronger by repetition.

decisions.choice: scepter of uprightness: a rule that is straight and just
decisions.reason: A scepter is the rod a king holds as the sign of his rule. εὐθύτης means "straightness", and so uprightness, justice: the Son rules rightly.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says
decisions.reason: The Greek has no verb; "he says" is carried over from verse 7. Balanced and Readable supply it.

decisions.choice: You rule your kingdom with what is right and fair.
alternatives: the scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom
decisions.reason: Readable explains the picture of the scepter as the way the king rules.

records.source: ἠγάπησας δικαιοσύνην καὶ ἐμίσησας ἀνομίαν· διὰ τοῦτο ἔχρισέν σε ὁ θεός, ὁ θεός σου, ἔλαιον ἀγαλλιάσεως παρὰ τοὺς μετόχους σου·
records.gloss: You loved righteousness and hated lawlessness; because of this anointed you the God, the God of you, [with] oil of exultation beyond the companions of you;
pieces: You have loved righteousness and hated lawlessness. For that reason God, {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} God, has anointed {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} with the oil of rejoicing and set {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} above {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} companions."

L.9: You loved righteousness and hated lawlessness; because of this God, {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} God, anointed {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} [with the] oil of exultation beyond {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} companions."

R.9: You have loved righteousness and hated evil. So God, {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} God, has anointed {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} as king and poured on {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} the oil of joy. He has honored {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} above all {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} companions."

decisions.choice: Psalm 45:8 (44:8 Greek), continued
decisions.reason: The quotation from Psalm 45 continues. The king who loves what is right is anointed by God above his fellows.

decisions.choice: God, your God: the subject who anoints
alternatives: therefore, O God, your God has anointed you
decisions.reason: The first θεός may be the subject ("God, your God, has anointed you") or, like verse 8, an address ("therefore, O God, your God has anointed you"). The Hebrew of Psalm 45:8 has the same ambiguity. Taking it as the subject is the simpler reading; the address would make the psalm call the Son "God" a second time.

decisions.choice: anointed with the oil of exultation: honored with festive oil, as kings were anointed
decisions.reason: Kings were anointed with oil when they took office (1 Samuel 16:13), and oil was poured on guests at feasts as a sign of joy (Psalm 23:5; Isaiah 61:3). The verb χρίω belongs to the same family as the title Christ, "the Anointed One".

decisions.choice: companions: those who share with him
decisions.reason: μέτοχος means "sharers, partners". In the psalm they are the king's fellows; Hebrews uses the same word for believers, who are "partners" in a heavenly calling (3:1) and in Christ (3:14).

decisions.choice: lawlessness: wickedness, contempt for God's law
decisions.reason: ἀνομία is literally "lawlessness", the opposite of the righteousness the king loves.

decisions.choice: anointed {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} as king and poured on {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} the oil of joy; honored {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} above
decisions.reason: Readable explains that anointing marked a king and that the oil was a sign of joy, and renders "beyond your companions" as being honored above them.

decisions.choice: evil
decisions.reason: Readable says "evil" for "lawlessness", a plainer word for what the king hates.

records.source: καί· Σὺ κατ’ ἀρχάς, κύριε, τὴν γῆν ἐθεμελίωσας, καὶ ἔργα τῶν χειρῶν σού εἰσιν οἱ οὐρανοί·
records.gloss: And, You in [the] beginnings, Lord, the earth founded, and works of the hands of you are the heavens;
pieces: And it also says, "Lord, at the beginning {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} founded the earth, and the heavens are what {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} hands have made.

L.10: And, "You, Lord, in [the] beginning laid the foundation of the earth, and the heavens are [the] works of {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} hands;

R.10: God also says to the Son, "Lord, in the beginning {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} made the earth and set it firmly in place. You made the skies with {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} own hands.

decisions.reason: Verses 10-12 quote Psalm 102:26-28 (101:26-28 in the Greek numbering) in the wording of the Greek translation. The psalm is the prayer of a sufferer who turns to the everlasting God, the Creator who outlasts heaven and earth.

decisions.choice: Lord: the Creator addressed in the psalm is here the Son
decisions.reason: The Greek psalm has "Lord" in this line, and the psalm as a whole is addressed to God by his name, YHWH (Psalm 102:2, 13), though the Hebrew of this line does not have the name. The author applies words spoken to the Creator God to the Son, as he said in verse 2 that God made the ages through him.

decisions.choice: the works of your hands
decisions.reason: "The work of your hands" is a common Old Testament way of speaking of what God has made (Psalm 8:7; 19:2).

decisions.choice: And it also says (B); God also says to the Son (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek has only "And," introducing the next quotation, still spoken "to the Son" (verse 8). Balanced and Readable supply a verb, and Readable names the speaker and the one addressed.

decisions.choice: made the earth and set it firmly in place; the skies
alternatives: laid the foundation of the earth
decisions.reason: Readable explains "laid the foundation" and uses "skies" for "the heavens" so that a young reader does not think of the place where God lives.

records.source: αὐτοὶ ἀπολοῦνται, σὺ δὲ διαμένεις· καὶ πάντες ὡς ἱμάτιον παλαιωθήσονται, καὶ ὡσεὶ περιβόλαιον ἑλίξεις αὐτούς, ὡς ἱμάτιον καὶ ἀλλαγήσονται· σὺ δὲ ὁ αὐτὸς εἶ, καὶ τὰ ἔτη σου οὐκ ἐκλείψουσιν.
records.gloss: They will perish, you but remain; and all like a garment will grow old, \v 12 and as a cloak you will roll up them, as a garment also they will be changed; you but the same are, and the years of you not will fail.
pieces: They will pass away, but {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} will remain. All of them will wear out as clothing does;

{{deity_pronoun:you|You}} will fold them up like a cloak, and like clothing they will be replaced. But {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are always the same, and {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} years will have no end."

L.11: they will perish, but {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} remain; and all will grow old like a garment,
L.12: and like a cloak {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} will roll them up, like a garment they will also be changed; but {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are the same, and {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} years will not fail."

R.11: The earth and the skies will come to an end, but {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} will always remain. They will all wear out like old clothes.
R.12: You will roll them up like a coat. Like clothes, they will be changed for new ones. But {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} never change, and {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} years will never come to an end."

decisions.choice: Psalm 102:27-28 (101:27-28 Greek), continued
decisions.reason: The quotation of Psalm 102 continues. Heaven and earth are like clothes that wear out and are put away; the Lord addressed in the psalm stays the same. The author has applied it to the Son (verse 10), whom he later calls "the same yesterday and today and forever" (13:8).

decisions.choice: "like a garment" repeated (SBLGNT)
alternatives: they will be changed (without "like a garment")
decisions.reason: The SBL text repeats "like a garment" before "they will also be changed", with the oldest manuscripts (P46, Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus). The Greek psalm and the later majority of manuscripts do not have the repeated phrase. Some manuscripts also read "you will change them" instead of "you will roll them up", as the Hebrew of Psalm 102:27 has it. The sense is the same. This description is from general knowledge; reviewers must check it against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: they will be changed: exchanged, like worn clothes taken off and replaced
decisions.reason: ἀλλάσσω means "change, exchange". The picture is of clothing taken off and replaced, so the created order will give way to something new (compare 12:26-28, where the shaken things are removed).

decisions.choice: you are the same: the Son does not change or come to an end
decisions.reason: "You are the same" sets the unchanging Lord against the changing creation. Applied to the Son, it says he shares God's eternity and faithfulness.

decisions.choice: replaced
decisions.reason: Balanced says "replaced" to make clear that the clothing picture is one of exchange (see m3); Literal keeps "changed", and Readable says "changed for new ones".

decisions.choice: The earth and the skies
decisions.reason: Readable names what "they" refers to, the earth and the heavens of verse 10.

records.source: πρὸς τίνα δὲ τῶν ἀγγέλων εἴρηκέν ποτε· Κάθου ἐκ δεξιῶν μου ἕως ἂν θῶ τοὺς ἐχθρούς σου ὑποπόδιον τῶν ποδῶν σου;
records.gloss: To which but of the angels has he said ever, Sit at [the] right of me until I put the enemies of you [as] a footstool of the feet of you?
pieces: Has God ever said to any of the angels, "Sit at {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} right hand, until I put {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} enemies under {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} feet as a footstool"?

L.13: But to which of the angels has {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} ever said, "Sit at {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} right [hand] until I put {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} enemies [as] a footstool of {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} feet"?

R.13: God never said to any angel, "Sit beside {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} at {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} right hand, in the place of honor, until I put {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} enemies under {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} feet like a footstool."

decisions.choice: Psalm 110:1 (109:1 Greek)
decisions.reason: The quotation is Psalm 110:1 (109:1 in the Greek numbering), already echoed in verse 3. In the Hebrew the words are spoken by YHWH: "The LORD says to my lord". The author quotes only what God says, and he returns to this psalm again and again (8:1; 10:12-13; 12:2). It is the Old Testament text most often quoted in the New Testament.

decisions.choice: a footstool for your feet: complete victory over enemies
decisions.reason: Conquerors put their feet on the necks of defeated kings (Joshua 10:24), and royal footstools were sometimes carved with figures of enemies. The picture is of total victory, still to be completed (10:13).

decisions.choice: a question expecting the answer "none"
decisions.reason: The question echoes verse 5 and closes the chain of quotations: God never said such words to any angel.

decisions.choice: Has God ever said to any of the angels
alternatives: To which of the angels has he ever said
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the question but turns it round to read naturally; Readable makes it the statement it implies, as in verse 5.

decisions.choice: beside {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} ... in the place of honor
decisions.reason: Readable explains what sitting at the king's right hand meant.

records.source: οὐχὶ πάντες εἰσὶν λειτουργικὰ πνεύματα εἰς διακονίαν ἀποστελλόμενα διὰ τοὺς μέλλοντας κληρονομεῖν σωτηρίαν;
records.gloss: Not all are they ministering spirits for service being sent out for the sake of those being about to inherit salvation?
pieces: Are not all the angels spirits in holy service, sent out to serve for the sake of those who are going to inherit salvation?

L.14: Are they not all ministering spirits, sent out for service for the sake of those who are about to inherit salvation?

R.14: All the angels are spirits who serve God. God sends them to help the people who are going to receive salvation.

decisions.choice: ministering spirits: spirits who serve in God's worship and work
decisions.reason: λειτουργικός comes from the word family of verse 7 ("ministers") and was used of sacred service in the temple. The angels serve; the Son sits enthroned (verse 13).

decisions.choice: about to inherit salvation: salvation as a coming inheritance
decisions.reason: Salvation here is the full deliverance believers will receive at the end (9:28), described as an inheritance, like the Son's in verses 2 and 4. μέλλω means "be about to, be going to".

decisions.choice: a question expecting the answer "yes"
decisions.reason: The question is rhetorical and expects agreement: angels are servants sent to help God's people.

decisions.choice: spirits in holy service
decisions.reason: Balanced brings out that the adjective belongs to the language of sacred service; "ministering" is a church word.

decisions.choice: statement instead of question; receive salvation
decisions.reason: Readable turns the rhetorical question into the statement it implies, and says "receive" for "inherit".
